title: Care and household work still divide time while socializing declines and digital leisure expands
source_unit: BLS American Time Use Survey respondents age 15 and over; published 2025 annual summary

denominator.unit: ATUS respondents age 15 and over; published annual estimates

household_activity_participation.unit: percent engaging in household activities on an average day

household_activity_time.value: women 2.8 hours and men 2.1 hours on days they did household activities

socializing_participation.unit: percent engaging in socializing and communicating on an average day

observations.method: BLS annual ATUS time-diary estimates with published subgroup and 2015 comparison tables; household work, socializing, and games/computer leisure are separate activity categories.
observations.uncertainty: These are population time-use averages, not a panel of the same people or evidence that digital leisure caused lower socializing. Activity categories do not measure quality, loneliness, care adequacy, or wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Women and men; adults living with children; age groups; all published ATUS respondents.
observations.counterinterpretation: Less reported socializing time can reflect survey classification, substitution into other forms of contact, age composition, work, health, or household constraints rather than cultural withdrawal.

denominator.unit: adults living with children under age 6 or under age 18, split by employment status

childcare_under_six.value: not-employed adults 3.3 hours versus employed adults 1.7 hours per day
childcare_under_six.unit: hours caring for and helping household children

household_activity_with_children.value: not-employed adults 3.1 hours versus employed adults 1.7 hours per day
household_activity_with_children.unit: hours of household activities among adults with children under 18

observations.method: ATUS published comparison of daily activity time by employment status among adults living with young children.
observations.uncertainty: Employment status is not randomly assigned and the release does not identify childcare availability, schedule control, income, care quality, or later work and household outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Adults living with children under age 6 or under age 18.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different time allocations may reflect choice, leave, unemployment, caregiving need, or household composition; they do not alone measure constraint or sacrifice.

boundary: This record adds a current time-allocation and cultural-participation layer. It does not establish a causal shift in social connection, care adequacy, economic security, health, trust, or political action. The federal shutdown interrupted part of 2025 ATUS collection and BLS describes the weighting adjustment and possible effect on estimates.
